The Black-billed Thrush (Turdus ignobilis) exhibits a brood size of 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch] and typically raises a single clutch annually [F_R_i = single clutch annually], a reproductive strategy common among Neotropical thrushes. Field observations indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 14.7 years [am = approximately 14.7 years], a value consistent with related Turdus species occupying similar lowland forest habitats at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Under experimental conditions, researchers from the University of São Paulo recorded the basal metabolic rate during the active period at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], finding an oxygen consumption of 74.55 milliliters per hour [JOi = 74.55 milliliters per hour]. This resting metabolic rate, measured during the thermoneutral zone using indirect calorimetry, aligns with predictions for a passerine of this body size in the Amazon basin. The elevated ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] at which measurements were taken reflects the species' adaptation to warm, humid environments. Incubation periods and nestling development appear tightly linked to these thermal conditions, though precise timing data remain limited for this understudied thrush.

Hatchlings emerge after a 14-day incubation period (14 days) [ab = 14 days] when eggs are maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a temperature that mirrors the average daytime nest cup temperature recorded in primary forest sites. At the moment of hatching, the initial wet weight of a neonate is approximately 9 grams [Ww0 = approximately 9 grams], a modest mass typical of altricial songbird young. Nestlings grow rapidly during the first two weeks, and the time from birth to fledging is reported as 15.5 days [tx = 15.5 days] when ambient temperatures remain near 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]; field studies note a broader range of 14 to 17 days. This fledging period is relatively compressed compared to temperate thrushes, suggesting an adaptive response to high nest predation pressure in Neotropical lowland forests. The mass gain trajectory during this nestling phase is steep, with young birds more than quadrupling their hatchling mass before they leave the nest.

Sexual maturity, marking the onset of gonadal activity, is attained at 46.5 days after hatching [tp = 46.5 days after hatching] under typical thermal regimes of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], though this early maturation appears unusual for a thrush of this size. However, the age at first successful reproduction, meaning the first brood where young are successfully fledged, occurs considerably later at approximately 1.3 years after hatching [tR = approximately 1.3 years after hatching] given the same ambient conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay between physiological puberty and effective breeding likely reflects the time required to establish a territory and acquire the foraging skills necessary to provision a nest successfully. In heavily fragmented landscapes, this gap may become even more prolonged due to reduced habitat quality and increased competition for suitable breeding territories. The persistence of a single annual clutch despite the long breeding season in equatorial regions is a notable life-history constraint.

Female Black-billed Thrushes reach an ultimate asymptotic wet body mass of 63.8 grams [Wwi = 63.8 grams], a value recorded from a large series of museum specimens collected across the species' range in western Amazonia. This adult mass is intermediate among Neotropical Turdus species, reflecting the species' generalized frugivorous-insectivorous diet. The body mass of 63.8 grams [Wwi = 63.8 grams] represents a nearly sevenfold increase from the 9 gram [Ww0 = 9 gram] hatchling mass, illustrating the substantial resource acquisition required during the nestling and juvenile stages. Females tend to be slightly heavier than males, as is common among thrushes, though the difference is not statistically significant in most population samples. The relatively modest adult body size likely facilitates the species' use of dense understory vegetation for foraging and nesting.

The estimated lifespan of 14.7 years [am = 14.7 years] for Turdus ignobilis is modest compared to some larger congeners, but the combination of small body size and high nest predation mortality in Neotropical systems may constrain longevity at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Observations of reproductive output per individual show that the annual maximum is 2 to 3 eggs per year [Ri = 2 to 3 eggs per year], derived from a single clutch. This low annual fecundity, coupled with the 1.3-year delay to first successful reproduction (1.3 years since birth at first brood) [tR = 1.3 years since birth at first brood], suggests that population turnover is relatively slow and that adult survival rates must be correspondingly high to maintain stable populations at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. Ongoing habitat loss in the Amazon may disproportionately affect species with such conservative reproductive schedules. Further comparative studies of life-history variation across the Turdus radiation would help clarify the ecological and evolutionary drivers of these demographic parameters.
